1.tip: ESD hurts bare chips. Handling a bare M.2 SSD stick = ESD risk. Plugging in displays or power supplies is not.
1.why: An M.2 SSD is a bare circuit board with exposed chips, so a static spark from your hand can damage it. The other choices don't involve touching sensitive parts inside the PC.

2.cue: new technical job, ESD be an issue
2.tip: Bare chips in your hand = ESD danger. The CPU is the most expensive chip you'll touch.
2.why: When you install a processor you handle a bare chip with many tiny pins or pads. Static from your body can silently damage it, so you wear a wrist strap.

3.tip: ESD question? Pick the choice where you hold a bare component inside the case: CPU, RAM, motherboard.
3.why: Installing a CPU means touching a static-sensitive chip directly. A UPS or speakers are plugged in from outside and don't expose bare circuits.

4.tip: Motherboard = big board full of chips. Touching it bare = ESD risk.
4.why: Replacing a motherboard means handling a board covered in sensitive chips and circuits, which static electricity can damage. Use an antistatic wrist strap and mat.

5.tip: RAM sticks are bare chips. Touch the gold edge carelessly and static can kill them.
5.why: RAM modules are exposed memory chips, and a static discharge you may not even feel can damage them. That's why you ground yourself before installing RAM.

6.cue: assemble a PC, ESD is an issue
6.tip: Building a PC? Every bare part you snap in (RAM, CPU) needs ESD care.
6.why: Assembling a PC means installing RAM by hand, and those memory chips are easily damaged by static. Ground yourself first with a wrist strap.

7.tip: Boot = BIOS/UEFI. The firmware wakes the PC up, not the CPU or bridges.
7.why: The BIOS or its newer version, UEFI, is firmware on a motherboard chip. It tests the hardware at power on and then finds and starts the operating system.

8.cue: upgrading an ATX motherboard with another
8.tip: New board, new socket. The old CPU may not fit, so you might have to buy one.
8.why: A new motherboard may use a different CPU socket or chipset, so your old CPU may not fit or work. ATX is just the board size, so the case is fine.

9.tip: Chipset = what the board CAN do. Ports and features like eSATA come from the chipset.
9.why: The chipset controls how the CPU talks to other parts and decides which features the motherboard supports, such as eSATA, USB types and RAM speeds.

10.tip: ROM = Read Only Memory. Read only means it can't be changed.
10.why: ROM holds permanent instructions, like old boot firmware. Its contents stay when power is off and normally can't be changed, so adapter cards still use it.

11.tip: DDR = Double Data Rate: data moves twice per clock tick.
11.why: DDR moves data on both the rising and falling edge of each clock cycle, so it transfers twice as much as plain SDRAM, which uses only one edge.

12.tip: Laser printer: the corona uses HIGH VOLTAGE and the fuser is HOT. Zap and burn.
12.why: Laser printers use thousands of volts to charge the drum and a fuser that heats to about 200 C to melt toner. Unplug and let it cool before working on it.

13.cue: screws externally through the PC case
13.tip: The power supply bolts in from the BACK of the case, where its plug and fan stick out.
13.why: The power supply sits at the back of the case with its power socket outside, so you screw it in from the outside. The motherboard, CPU and RAM mount inside.

14.tip: Modern drive data cable = SATA. ATX is power, PWR_SW is the button.
14.why: Internal hard drives use a SATA data cable to the SATA port on the motherboard. ATX is the main power connector and PWR_SW is the front power button header.

15.tip: Video cards go in the long expansion slots: section D in the picture.
15.why: In the picture, section D holds the PCIe expansion slots where add-in cards like a video card go. A is power, B is SATA ports and C is the RAM slots.

16.cue: connected to the motherboard with a SATA cable
16.tip: SATA = storage: hard drives and optical (DVD) drives.
16.why: SATA cables connect drives, like hard drives and DVD optical drives, to the motherboard. Cards plug into slots and the power supply uses power cables.

17.cue: hardware failure detected by the BIOS
17.tip: POST talks in beeps. Beep codes tell you which part failed.
17.why: During POST the BIOS checks the hardware. If something fails before the screen works, it plays a beep code, a pattern of beeps that points to the bad part.

18.cue: BIOS settings to secure a computer
18.tip: BIOS security: Passwords, TPM chip, drive encryption. MAC filtering and TKIP are wireless router stuff.
18.why: In BIOS/UEFI you can set boot and setup passwords, turn on the TPM security chip and enable drive encryption. MAC filtering and TKIP are set on wireless routers.

19.tip: RAID = many drives working as a team, for safety (redundancy) or speed.
19.why: A RAID adapter links several drives so they act as one, either copying data for protection if a drive fails, or spreading data out for faster speed.

20.tip: Paste goes between the hot chip and its cooler: CPU and heat sink.
20.why: Thermal paste fills tiny air gaps between the CPU and the heat sink so heat moves well from the chip into the cooler.

21.cue: purpose of a Safety Data Sheet
21.tip: SDS = Safety Data Sheet = how to handle Dangerous Stuff.
21.why: A Safety Data Sheet explains a chemical's dangers and how to handle, store, clean up and dispose of it safely, like toner or cleaning solvents.

22.cue: cleaning the inside of a computer
22.tip: Cleaning removes dust. Dust traps heat and makes parts overheat.
22.why: Dust builds up on fans and heat sinks and blocks airflow, which makes parts run hot. Cleaning the inside removes it. EMI and ESD aren't fixed by cleaning.

23.tip: Can of air: keep it UPRIGHT, or liquid sprays out. Hold the fans still.
23.why: Tilting a can of compressed air can spray freezing liquid onto parts. Also hold fans still so they don't spin too fast, and never use window cleaner on LCDs.

24.tip: Factory with wood dust? Dust is the laptop killer: it clogs vents and fans.
24.why: Wood dust gets sucked into the laptop vents and clogs fans and heat sinks, causing overheating. The warmth and humidity are high but still within normal limits.

25.cue: testing did not identify an exact cause
25.tip: Theory failed? Make a NEW theory and WRITE DOWN what you tried.
25.why: If a test doesn't find the cause, you go back and form a new theory. Documenting each test stops you from repeating it and helps others later.

26.cue: set to 230 volts, outlet in the United States
26.tip: Too LITTLE voltage = nothing happens. Set to 230 V but fed 120 V means the PC won't start.
26.why: US outlets give about 120 V. A power supply set for 230 V gets only about half the voltage it expects, so it can't power up the PC. Too much voltage is the dangerous case.

27.tip: LAN = Local Area Network: one building or campus. WAN = wide, MAN = city, PAN = personal.
27.why: A LAN covers a small area like one building or campus, run by one organization. A WAN spans large distances and a MAN covers a city.

28.tip: Wired + fast = cable (TV coax) and DSL (phone line). Dial-up is wired but slow.
28.why: Cable Internet uses the TV coaxial cable and DSL uses phone lines, both wired and high speed. Satellite and cellular are wireless, and dial-up is very slow.

29.tip: UDP = fast and no promises. TCP = slower but guaranteed.
29.why: UDP skips the acknowledgments and ordering that TCP does, so it's faster with less overhead. Use it when speed matters more than every packet arriving, like voice or video.

30.tip: DHCP hands out IP addresses automatically. No more typing them by hand.
30.why: A DHCP server gives each workstation its IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS automatically, so you don't set them manually on every computer.

31.tip: UTM = Unified Threat Management: firewall + VPN + IDS/IPS + DoS protection in one box.
31.why: A UTM appliance combines many security features, like firewall, VPN, intrusion detection and prevention and DoS protection, in a single device. TPM is a chip in a PC.

32.tip: 169.254 = APIPA = 'I asked DHCP and nobody answered.'
32.why: When Windows can't reach a DHCP server, it gives itself an APIPA address starting with 169.254. That address only works locally, so there's no Internet.

33.tip: Basic trio: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway. (DNS helps with names, but isn't one of the three.)
33.why: The IP address identifies the PC, the subnet mask shows which addresses are local, and the default gateway is the router used to reach other networks.

34.tip: /64 = first 4 groups are network, last 4 groups are the host.
34.why: A /64 prefix means the first 64 bits (4 groups) are the network part. The last 4 groups, 0607:1234:aa10:ba01, identify the host itself.

35.tip: Apps use ports. Block the port in Windows Firewall to block the app.
35.why: Network apps listen on specific TCP or UDP ports. Blocking those ports in Windows Firewall stops traffic from reaching the app. MAC filtering is a router feature.

36.tip: Wi-Fi calling = calls over Wi-Fi when the cell signal is weak.
36.why: Wi-Fi calling routes phone calls over a Wi-Fi network instead of the cell tower, so it helps most where the cellular signal is poor, like inside some buildings.

37.tip: Laptop parts are small and custom. They don't fit desktops.
37.why: Laptop parts are built small and often proprietary, so most won't work in a desktop. Laptop boards have no standard size, and laptop CPUs do need cooling.

38.cue: bridge between laptop hardware and the operating system
38.tip: ACPI = Advanced Configuration and Power Interface: the Power Interface.
38.why: ACPI is the standard that lets the operating system control hardware power states, like sleep and hibernate, so you can set power management schemes.

39.tip: Customer can swap the easy stuff: battery and RAM. Leave screens and internal cards to the tech.
39.why: Batteries and RAM are usually reached through an outside cover or latch, so users can replace them. Screens, card readers and Mini-PCIe cards need a technician.

40.tip: Big media sync = fast links: Wi-Fi or a USB cable.
40.why: Syncing apps, movies and music moves lots of data, so it's done over a USB cable or Wi-Fi. Bluetooth and NFC are too slow, and cellular costs data.

41.tip: Inkjet: cheap to buy, wet ink. Laser: dry toner, fused by heat.
41.why: Inkjets cost less to buy at first. Laser printers melt dry toner onto the paper, so pages come out dry, while inkjet ink can still be wet and smear.

42.cue: collate option and prints two copies
42.why: Collating prints each copy as a full set in order, so you get pages 1, 2, 3 and then 1, 2, 3 again. Without collate you'd get 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3.

43.cue: printing takes too long, graphics and photographs
43.tip: Big pictures need memory. More printer RAM = faster big jobs.
43.why: Graphics and photos make large print jobs. More printer RAM lets the printer hold and process the whole page faster instead of waiting on data.

44.cue: Windows print server services to MAC OS
44.tip: Bonjour = Apple's 'hello' service that lets Windows share printers with Macs.
44.why: Bonjour Print Server is Apple software you install on Windows so the Windows PC can share its printers with Mac clients. AirPrint is for Apple devices printing directly.

45.tip: Maintenance kit = parts that wear: fuser and rollers (pickup + transfer).
45.why: Parts that wear out with use, like the fuser assembly and the pickup and transfer rollers, come in the kit. Coronas and paper trays usually aren't included.

46.tip: Damp air = damp paper = paper jams.
46.why: Paper soaks up moisture from humid air, so it sticks together and curls, which causes jams. A test page jamming points to the paper, not the driver or cables.

47.cue: host multiple operating systems on a single CPU
47.tip: Many OSes on one physical server = virtualization.
47.why: Virtualization runs several virtual machines, each with its own OS, on one physical server, so each customer gets a web server without buying separate hardware.

48.tip: VMs don't care what hardware they land on. Restore anywhere.
48.why: A virtual machine runs on a hypervisor, not directly on the hardware, so you can restore it on any server without needing an exact hardware match.

49.tip: Data center = Type 1 (bare metal): ESXi and Hyper-V. Desktop apps like VirtualBox are Type 2.
49.why: VMware ESXi and Hyper-V are Type 1 hypervisors that run directly on server hardware, which suits data centers. Virtual PC, Fusion and VirtualBox run on top of a desktop OS.

50.cue: opens them in different virtual desktops
50.tip: Windows 10 lets you make several desktops (Task View). That's Windows Virtual Desktop.
50.why: Windows 10 lets you create multiple virtual desktops on the same computer and put different apps on each one, then switch between them.

51.tip: PaaS = Platform for building apps. SaaS = use apps. IaaS = rent servers.
51.why: Platform as a Service gives developers the tools and environment to build, test and deliver apps over the web, without managing the servers underneath.

52.tip: SDRAM is synchronized with the clock, so it can pipeline: overlapping work in parallel.
52.why: SDRAM runs in sync with the system clock, which lets it pipeline commands so it handles overlapping instructions at the same time. Two reads and writes per cycle is DDR.

53.tip: After a power outage, check power first: the external RAID box may be off.
53.why: An external RAID controller has its own power. After an outage it may not have come back on, so the server can't see it and reports RAID not found.

54.cue: touch screen that is not working correctly
54.tip: Touch screen slow or odd? Start simple: close apps first, then think hardware.
54.why: With too many apps open, the device runs short of memory and processing power, so taps can lag or register wrong. Closing apps is the first easy fix to try.

55.cue: sharing printers in a corporate environment
55.tip: Shared printer risks: who can print (authentication) and what it remembers (cached files).
55.why: Without user authentication anyone can use or misuse the printer, and cached print files stored on the printer can leak private documents.

56.tip: Assess = look at the impact on the business before the change.
56.why: The assessment step studies how a proposed change will affect business processes, its risks and cost, before anyone approves or carries it out.

57.why: RAID 10 mirrors pairs of drives for safety and then stripes data across the pairs for speed, combining RAID 1 and RAID 0.

58.tip: RAID 1 = one copy, the mirror image.
58.why: RAID 1 writes the same data to two drives, a mirror. If one drive fails, the other still has everything.

59.tip: RAID 5 = stripes + one parity. Needs 3+ drives.
59.why: RAID 5 spreads data across drives with parity info, so the array can rebuild data if any one drive fails.

60.tip: RAID 0 = zero protection, just striping for speed.
60.why: RAID 0 splits data across drives for speed but keeps no copy or parity, so one failed drive loses everything.

61.tip: RAID 6 = RAID 5 with double parity. Survives 2 drive failures.
61.why: RAID 6 stores two sets of parity, so the array keeps working even if two drives fail at the same time.

62.tip: Batteries contain toxic metals: always recycle by local rules.
62.why: Batteries contain toxic metals that can harm people and the environment, so they must be recycled following local regulations, never thrown away or burned.

63.tip: E-waste rule: recycle it, following local regulations.
63.why: Monitors can hold hazardous materials like lead or mercury, so they go to approved e-waste recycling as local rules require.

64.cue: dispose of an old power supply
64.tip: Any computer part? Recycle following local regulations. Never burn or bury.
64.why: Power supplies contain metals and components that shouldn't go in a landfill. Recycling them by local rules keeps hazardous materials out of the environment.

65.tip: Circuit boards are e-waste: recycle them by local rules.
65.why: RAM is a circuit board with metals and chemicals, so it counts as e-waste and should be recycled following local regulations.

66.why: Motherboards contain lead solder and other hazardous materials, so they must go to e-waste recycling according to local regulations.

67.cue: dispose of an old hard drive
67.tip: Hard drive: wipe the data, then recycle by local rules.
67.why: Hard drives are e-waste and should be recycled following local regulations, after you make sure any data on them is securely wiped or destroyed.

68.tip: Random reboots = Power or heat: PSU and CPU.
68.why: A failing power supply can drop power and restart the PC, and an overheating CPU makes the system shut down or reboot to protect itself.

69.why: Unstable power from a bad power supply, or a CPU that overheats, are the classic causes of a computer rebooting on its own.

70.cue: reboots several times before it eventually starts
70.tip: Keeps rebooting? Suspect PSU and CPU first.
70.why: If the power supply can't deliver steady power, or the CPU is overheating or failing, the PC can restart over and over before it finally boots.

71.cue: working on a spreadsheet, the computer reboots
71.tip: Sudden reboot in the middle of work = PSU or CPU.
71.why: A sudden reboot while working usually means the power supply briefly failed or the CPU overheated and the system shut down to protect itself.

72.why: NetBIOS over TCP/IP uses ports 137 to 139 for names and sessions on older Windows networks. SMB runs on 445 and HTTPS on 443.

73.why: SSH uses port 22 to give a secure, encrypted remote command line. Telnet does the same job on port 23 but without encryption.

74.why: IMAP uses port 143 to let email clients read mail that stays on the server.

75.why: Telnet uses port 23 for remote command line access. It sends everything in plain text, which is why SSH on port 22 replaced it.

76.why: SNMP, Simple Network Management Protocol, uses UDP port 161 so management software can monitor and manage network devices.

77.tip: LDAP = 389: the directory lookup (like Active Directory).
77.why: LDAP uses port 389 to look up users, computers and other objects in a directory service like Active Directory.

78.why: SMTP uses port 25 to send email between mail servers and from clients to servers.

79.tip: SLP = 427: Service Location Protocol finds services like printers.
79.why: SLP, Service Location Protocol, uses port 427 so devices can find services on the local network, like printers, without manual setup.

80.why: DNS uses port 53 to translate names like www.example.com into IP addresses. DHCP uses 67/68 and TFTP uses 69.

81.tip: Two rules: drop leading zeros in each group, and swap ONE run of all-zero groups for ::.
81.why: Remove leading zeros (0db8 to db8, 0008 to 8, 0001 to 1) and replace the three 0000 groups with :: to get 2001:db8::a0b0:8:1.

82.tip: Use :: for the LONGEST run of zeros. A single 0000 becomes just 0.
82.why: Drop leading zeros (09ea to 9ea, 0fe0 to fe0, 0290 to 290). The lone 0000 becomes 0, and the two zero groups in a row become ::.

83.tip: Only LEADING zeros go. Trailing zeros (c400) stay.
83.why: Drop leading zeros (0042 to 42, 0010 to 10, 0909 to 909), keep c400 as it is, and replace the three 0000 groups with ::.

84.tip: One zero group can still be written as ::. Leading zeros drop, trailing ones stay.
84.why: Drop leading zeros in each group (0420 to 420, 00c4 to c4, 0025 to 25, 0190 to 190, 0990 to 990) and replace the single 0000 group with ::.

85.tip: Two zero runs? Use :: for the longer one, write the other as 0.
85.why: The two 0000 groups after db8 become ::. The later single 0000 becomes 0. Leading zeros drop (0ab8 to ab8, 0001 to 1), but 1000 keeps its zeros.

86.tip: Three zero groups after fe80 collapse to ::. Then trim leading zeros.
86.why: The three 0000 groups become ::, and leading zeros drop (0220 to 220, 0b3f to b3f, 0029 to 29), giving fe80::220:b3f:f0e0:29.

87.tip: Only one :: is allowed per address. Other zero groups become 0.
87.why: Both 0000 groups are single, so one becomes :: and the other is written 0. Leading zeros drop (00bf to bf, 00e0 to e0) while 9ea0 keeps its trailing zero.

88.cue: contents of RAM have been saved to a temporary file
88.tip: S4 = hibernate: RAM saved to disk, power off.
88.why: In S4, hibernate, the PC copies RAM to a file on the hard drive and powers off. When you turn it on, the saved state is loaded back.

89.tip: S1 = lightest sleep: CPU and RAM still powered.
89.why: S1 is the lightest sleep state: the CPU and RAM keep power and only unused devices turn off, so it wakes very quickly.

90.cue: CPU is off, but the RAM is refreshed
90.tip: S2 = CPU off, RAM still refreshed. One step deeper than S1.
90.why: In S2 the CPU is turned off but the RAM keeps being refreshed so its contents stay. It's deeper than S1 but lighter than S3.

91.tip: S5 = soft off. S0 = on. Count up as it goes deeper.
91.why: S5 is the soft off state: the computer is shut down and nothing is saved, though the power supply still gives a little power for wake-up.

92.tip: S3 = Suspend to RAM (Sleep). S4 = suspend to disk.
92.why: S3, suspend to RAM, turns off the CPU and keeps RAM on slow refresh using little power. It's the normal sleep mode most people use.

93.cue: computer is on and the CPU is running
93.why: S0 is the working state: the computer is fully on and the CPU is running normally.

94.tip: Big photo jobs crawl? Give the printer more RAM.
94.why: High resolution photos create huge print jobs. More RAM in the printer lets it hold and process each page faster. Ribbons are only for impact printers.

95.cue: deep in a mine, paper constantly jams
95.tip: Mine = damp. Damp paper = jams. Move to drier air.
95.why: Mines are very humid, and paper absorbs moisture, then sticks and curls and jams. Moving the printer to a drier place fixes it.

96.tip: Streaks? Shake the toner cartridge to spread the toner out.
96.why: When toner clumps or runs low in parts of the cartridge, the page gets streaks. Gently rocking the cartridge spreads the toner evenly again.

97.cue: not showing up on the list of available printers
97.tip: Can't find the printer? Add it by its IP address.
97.why: If automatic discovery doesn't find a network printer, you can add it manually by typing its IP address so the computer knows where to send jobs.

98.tip: Jobs go out but never print? They're going out the wrong port.
98.why: If the printer driver points to the wrong port, jobs are sent somewhere the printer isn't listening. Changing the port in printer properties fixes it.

99.cue: colors are different from the colors on screens
99.tip: Screen and paper colors don't match? Calibrate.
99.why: Calibration adjusts the printer so its colors line up with what you see on screen, by aligning heads and correcting color output.

100.cue: preventive maintenance, printer no longer available
100.tip: After maintenance, check the basics first: is it plugged in?
100.why: After maintenance the printer may have been left unplugged or turned off. Checking power is the simplest first step before anything else.

101.tip: Faded print = low toner. Replace the cartridge.
101.why: When the toner cartridge runs low, not enough toner reaches the page, so prints look faded. A new cartridge fixes it.

102.tip: Failed to print = can't REACH the printer: share removed or cable loose.
102.why: This message means the job couldn't reach the printer. That happens if the shared printer was unshared or if a cable is loose or unplugged.

103.tip: Garbage characters = bad translation (driver) or bad link (loose cable).
103.why: The driver translates documents into the printer's language. A wrong or old driver, or a loose cable that garbles data, makes strange characters print.

104.tip: Wrong colors? Check heads (clean + calibrate) and cartridges (right one installed?).
104.why: Clogged or misaligned print heads mix colors badly, and the wrong cartridge puts the wrong ink or toner where a color should go.

105.tip: Faded = not enough toner, or paper that won't take it.
105.why: Low toner means less reaches the page, and paper that doesn't suit the printer may not hold the toner well, so print looks faded.

106.tip: Blank panel? Is it on? Is the contrast turned down?
106.why: A blank control panel usually means the printer is off, or the screen's contrast is set so low you can't see anything.

107.tip: Creased paper = paper problem: loose tray guides or paper loaded wrong.
107.why: If the tray guides aren't snug against the paper, or the paper is loaded wrong, it feeds at an angle and gets creased on its way through.

108.tip: Impact printer + faded = ribbon (worn or damaged).
108.why: Impact printers strike an inked ribbon against the paper. When the ribbon is worn out or damaged, there's not enough ink and the characters look faint.

109.tip: Won't feed? Bad paper (wrinkled) or wrong size set.
109.why: Wrinkled paper won't pick up cleanly, and if the printer expects a different paper size than what's loaded, it won't feed from that tray.

110.cue: NVMe drive (C:) and a mechanical hard drive (D:)
110.tip: Missing drive? Look in Disk Management: the OS's view of every disk.
110.why: Disk Management shows every drive Windows can see, even ones without a drive letter or partition, so it tells you if the OS recognizes the disk.

111.cue: save an email attachment, D: drive not an option
111.tip: Quick check: open File Explorer and see if the drive is listed.
111.why: File Explorer lists the drives Windows has mounted. If D: shows there, the OS sees it. Ping, ipconfig and web browsers test networks, not drives.

112.cue: drive, present in the save options yesterday
112.tip: Device Manager = does Windows see the hardware?
112.why: Device Manager lists the hardware Windows detects and shows errors on devices, so you can check if the drive is recognized and its driver works.

113.cue: SSD for the operating system, mechanical hard drive
113.tip: Is the drive there? File Explorer shows it at a glance.
113.why: File Explorer shows all drives Windows has mounted. If the data drive is listed there, the OS recognizes it. Swapping cables is a hardware step, not an OS check.

114.cue: data can no longer be saved [Case 2]
114.tip: OS check for hardware = Device Manager (look under Disk drives).
114.why: Device Manager shows whether Windows detects the drive and whether its driver has a problem. ipconfig and browsers only test network settings.

115.tip: GPS dead? The location service may be turned off.
115.why: GPS depends on the location service. If that service is disabled in settings, GPS won't work even though the hardware is fine.

116.tip: App stuck? Restart the app. Then the device, if needed.
116.why: An app that won't load may be frozen in the background. Closing and restarting it clears its state and usually fixes the problem.

117.tip: Not responding = force close and restart the app.
117.why: When an app hangs, restarting it clears whatever it got stuck on. Screen and GPU problems don't cause a single app to freeze.

118.tip: Can't decrypt = missing the key. Keys live in digital certificates.
118.why: Encrypted email is unlocked with a key from a digital certificate. If that certificate is missing from the device, the email can't be decrypted.

119.tip: Gibberish on the page? Reinstall the printer driver.
119.why: The printer driver translates documents into commands the printer understands. A corrupt driver sends bad commands, so strange characters print.

120.tip: 'Memory overload' says it: add more memory to the printer.
120.why: Large documents can be bigger than the printer's memory can hold. Adding memory lets it store and process the whole job.

121.tip: Airplane mode turns off the radios, GPS included.
121.why: Airplane mode switches off the device's wireless radios, including GPS, so location stops working until you turn airplane mode off.

123.tip: Blank pages from a laser printer? Out of toner: replace the cartridge.
123.why: If the toner cartridge is empty (or its seal tape wasn't removed), no toner reaches the page, so it comes out blank.

124.tip: Two OSes on one PC: dual boot (pick at startup) or a VM (run side by side).
124.why: Dual boot installs both OSes and you choose one at startup. Client-side virtualization runs another OS in a virtual machine on your workstation.

125.cue: Windows for file and printer sharing
125.tip: SMB = Share My Bits: Windows file and printer sharing.
125.why: SMB, Server Message Block, is the protocol Windows uses to share files and printers on a network. SMTP and IMAP are for email.

126.tip: VA = Very deep blacks: crystals tilt Vertically for high contrast.
126.why: VA panels tilt their liquid crystals vertically, which blocks light well and gives deep blacks and a high contrast ratio compared to TN and IPS.

127.tip: SMB = Windows file sharing (and printer sharing).
127.why: SMB lets Windows computers share files, folders and printers over the network. Web browsing uses HTTP and email uses SMTP or IMAP.

128.cue: six stages of the troubleshooting process
128.tip: I Eat Tacos, Eat Very Delicious: Identify, Establish theory, Test, Establish plan, Verify, Document.
128.why: You first identify the problem, guess a cause, and test it. Then you plan and apply the fix, verify everything works, and finally document what you did.

129.cue: Match the memory type to the feature
129.tip: DDR 184 pins. DDR2 240 pins at 1.8 V. DDR3 240 pins at 1.5 V. DDR4 288 pins. Newer = lower voltage.
129.why: Each DDR generation changed the module: DDR has 184 pins, DDR2 and DDR3 both have 240 pins but DDR3 uses less power (1.5 V vs 1.8 V), and DDR4 has 288 pins.

130.cue: Match the problem to the possible solution
130.tip: Swollen capacitors = new board. New CPU not fully seen = BIOS update. New video card, no video = plug in its power.
130.why: Bulging capacitors mean the board is failing. A BIOS update adds support for a new CPU. Big PCIe video cards need their own power cable. Fans with no beeps point to a bad cable or seated part.
